title: The Name remains
hook: naam rahio saadhoo rahio: the Name remains, the holy remain, the Guru remains (Salok M9 56, ang 1429)

segments.voice: Yesterday: tek, and your line: he remains. Did you do one staying thing for someone in a hard stretch? After a run of saloks about what goes, today's is about what stays. Day six hundred seven.

For a week now these saloks have been taking things away. Rama and Ravana, gone. Youth, gone. Strength, gone. Friends, gone. Whatever is born will pass, today or tomorrow. A listener could be forgiven for wondering whether the ninth Guru was simply very sad. Then comes salok fifty-six, and the whole list turns over. After all that subtraction, he finally names what doesn't go. It's three things, said in one breath, each with the same verb. And then a sting in the tail about how few people notice them. Today: the Name remains.
screen: `A WEEK OF THINGS TAKEN AWAY.` → `THE LIST TURNS OVER.` → `THREE THINGS THAT DON'T GO.`

segments.voice: Salok fifty-six, Ang fourteen twenty-nine. Naam rahio, saadhoo rahio, rahio gur gobind. Rahio means remained, stayed, abides. The Name remains. The saadhoo, the holy one, the true devotee, remains. The Guru, God, remains. Three things, one verb, like three posts driven into ground that everything else is washing over. Take them one at a time. The Name, naam, stands at the center of Sikh devotion: God's presence, remembered and repeated. The saadhoo is the person who lives in that remembrance. Gurbani speaks often of the saadh sangat, the company of such people, and of how their example outlasts them. And gur gobind here isn't the tenth Guru's name: in this line it's God as Guru, the teacher who is also the Lord. The second line is the sting. In paraphrase: Nanak says, in this world, how rare is the one who has repeated the Guru's mantra. So the three things that last are there for anyone, and the salok says few pick them up. That's the shape of the whole salok collection. All week the world was a dream, a show, a wall of sand. That wasn't gloom for its own sake. It was clearing the table so you could see what was still on it. Read this way, the salok answers the rest. Everything on the table passes. The Name, the people who live it, and God are still there when the table is cleared.
screen: `RAHIO: IT REMAINED.` · `THE NAME, THE HOLY, THE GURU.` · `GUR GOBIND HERE: GOD AS GURU.` · `HOW RARE THE ONE WHO REPEATS IT.` · then, large: `THE NAME REMAINS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name what remains for you. Sit, and let your breath slow. Think back over the things these saloks took away: youth, strength, friends who drifted. Then ask a different question: what has stayed? Maybe a faith, maybe a person who's always been there, maybe a practice, maybe a line like this one. Name one thing, quietly, to yourself. If you pray, you can repeat Waheguru slowly, as one way of picking up what remains. The bell holds the time.
Rahio, remains, stays, abides. Naam rahio, saadhoo rahio, rahio gur gobind: the Name, the holy, and God as Guru all rahio when everything else goes.
Your line: still there when it's cleared. When something today reminds you that things pass, say the line once and think of the one thing you named. Day six hundred seven.

howItsDone: Salok fifty-six is read near the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teachers present it as the answer to the saloks about passing.

fork.setup: after a week of saloks taking things away, what does salok fifty-six do?
options: names what remains: the Name, the holy, the Guru.
fork.reveal: the list turns over. all the passing was clearing the table so you could see what was still on it.

original.note: Gurmukhi: saadhoo, the holy one, a devotee who lives in the Name; one of the three things that remain.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Name remains is a comforting phrase.
what it means: it's the answer to a week of loss: the Name, the holy and God stay.
what a scholar hears: three clauses share the verb rahio; gur gobind is read as God-as-Guru, and the closing line on how few repeat the gur mant gives the salok its edge.

sources.ref: Salok Mahalla 9, salok 56 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer guesses what the listener wondered and drops 'second to last' (a count); 'the whole of Sikh devotion' and 'almost nobody' softened to what the salok says; removed the bhog-after-a-death ending, which is day 609's whole lesson.
Transliteration naam rahio saadhoo rahio rahio gur gobind / kahu naanak ih jagat mai kin japio gur mant: confirm.
Reading of gur gobind as God-as-Guru rather than Guru Gobind Singh: confirm this is the standard reading.
Second line rendered 'how rare the one who has repeated the Guru's mantra': confirm sense of kin.
